clinicalPearls: HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome of uncontrolled immune activation: over-activated CD8 T cells and macrophages drive a cytokine storm and widespread hemophagocytosis (immune cells engulfing blood cells), producing fever, cytopenias and organ injury rather than effective clearance of the trigger.

Two broad forms exist — primary/familial HLH from inherited defects of lymphocyte cytotoxicity (e.g. perforin/PRF1, UNC13D), usually presenting in infants and children; and secondary/acquired HLH triggered by infection (classically EBV), malignancy (especially lymphoma), or autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease, where it is termed macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).

The clinical hallmark is persistent high fever that does NOT respond to antibiotics, with hepatosplenomegaly and progressive cytopenias affecting two or more lineages — a picture that closely mimics severe sepsis but fails to resolve with antimicrobials alone.

A markedly elevated serum ferritin is the most useful bedside clue: values in the tens of thousands are strongly suggestive in adults, and a rising ferritin with falling cell counts and falling fibrinogen should prompt urgent evaluation.

Diagnosis commonly uses the HLH-2004 framework (five or more of eight features): fever; splenomegaly; cytopenias in two or more lineages; hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia; hemophagocytosis on marrow, spleen or lymph node; low or absent NK-cell activity; ferritin at or above 500 micrograms/L; and elevated soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor). The H-score is an alternative probability tool for secondary HLH in adults.
harrison.pathophysiology: Defective or overwhelmed cytotoxic lymphocyte function fails to clear antigen-presenting and infected cells, so antigen persists and continuously stimulates CD8+ T cells and macrophages. The result is unrestrained secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (notably interferon-gamma, IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-18) — a cytokine storm — that activates macrophages to phagocytose erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets (hemophagocytosis) in the marrow and reticuloendothelial system. This drives the cardinal features: fever from systemic inflammation, cytopenias from marrow consumption and hemophagocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly and transaminitis from organ infiltration, hyperferritinemia and hypertriglyceridemia from macrophage activation, and hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy that can progress to disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Severe sepsis / septic shock — the principal mimic, with overlapping fever, cytopenias and organ dysfunction
Disseminated infection (EBV, CMV and other viruses; tuberculosis; visceral leishmaniasis; severe rickettsial disease)
Lymphoma and other haematological malignancies, which can both trigger and mimic HLH
Adult-onset Still's disease and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis complicated by macrophage activation syndrome
Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) and other causes of fever with cytopenias
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
infectionMimics: Severe rickettsial or scrub typhus infection
nonInfectiousMimics: Adult-onset Still's disease / systemic JIA with macrophage activation syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin — very high values (often above 10,000 micrograms/L in adults) are highly suggestive
Fasting triglycerides and fibrinogen (hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia)
Full blood count with film (bi- or tri-lineage cytopenias)
Soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor) and NK-cell activity where available
Bone marrow aspirate / biopsy for hemophagocytosis (may be absent early — a normal marrow does NOT exclude HLH)
Liver function tests and coagulation profile (transaminitis, coagulopathy / DIC)
Trigger work-up: EBV / CMV and other viral PCR, blood cultures, and evaluation for lymphoma and autoimmune disease
H-score calculation to estimate the probability of secondary HLH in adults
redFlags: Persistent high fever unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics with worsening cytopenias
Extreme hyperferritinemia (tens of thousands) with falling fibrinogen — impending decompensation
Rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction, coagulopathy or DIC
Neurological involvement (seizures, altered sensorium) indicating CNS-HLH
Underlying lymphoma or EBV-driven disease, which carry high mortality and need urgent trigger-directed therapy
pitfalls: Anchoring on 'sepsis' and continuing antibiotics while HLH progresses — suspect HLH when a septic picture does not improve and the ferritin is very high.
Assuming a normal early bone marrow excludes HLH; hemophagocytosis can appear later, and the diagnosis is clinical plus biochemical, not marrow-dependent.
Treating the syndrome without an aggressive search for the trigger (infection, malignancy, autoimmune) — outcome depends on identifying and treating it.
Over-relying on a ferritin of 500 micrograms/L alone, which is not specific; it is the very high values and the overall pattern that matter.
harrison.prognosis: Untreated HLH is frequently fatal. Outcome depends on prompt recognition, the underlying trigger (malignancy- and EBV-associated disease carry the worst prognosis), and timely trigger-directed and immunosuppressive therapy. Macrophage activation syndrome arising in rheumatic disease generally has a better prognosis when recognised and treated early.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — histiocytic / hemophagocytic syndromes
H-score for reactive haemophagocytic syndrome (Fardet et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2014)
management: Suppress the hyperinflammatory cytokine storm promptly with immunochemotherapy combining etoposide and dexamethasone, with ciclosporin, while identifying the trigger
Direct therapy at the underlying cause: rituximab for EBV-driven disease, treatment of the causative lymphoma or malignancy, or control of the underlying rheumatic disorder
For macrophage activation syndrome, use pulsed corticosteroids with anakinra (IL-1 blockade) and consider ciclosporin
Consider emapalumab (interferon-gamma blockade) for refractory or primary familial disease
Provide supportive care for cytopenias, coagulopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation, plus prophylaxis and treatment of infection
Refer primary or familial HLH for allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only curative option, and offer genetic counselling and family testing
Monitor ferritin, blood counts, fibrinogen and organ function, watch for CNS involvement, and escalate to intensive care for multi-organ failure
